positions.statement: Evaluating an LLM system is different from evaluating an LLM model — you must evaluate your own system on the task it is meant to solve, not just the base model.

sources.quote: evaluating LLM systems is not the same as evaluating LLM models, which is usually done through benchmarks
sources.statement: LLM system evaluation is different from LLM model evaluation, which is typically done via public benchmarks.

sources.quote: if you're building a specific application like a chatbot or even a simpler prompt chain you need to test it on the tasks that it is meant to solve
sources.statement: If you build a specific application (e.g., a chatbot or prompt chain), you need to test the whole system on the tasks it's meant to solve, not just the underlying model.

sources.quote: [illustrative] benchmarks tell you about the model, evals tell you about your product
sources.statement: [illustrative] System-level evaluation matters more than model benchmarks.

sources.quote: [illustrative] stop shipping on vibes; measure the system you actually built
sources.statement: [illustrative] Teams should evaluate their assembled system, not the raw model.

positions.statement: For a specialized system (e.g. RAG), build your own evaluation rather than reaching for an off-the-shelf public benchmark.

sources.quote: So if you are building a RAG system don't search for a RAG benchmark - build your own.
sources.statement: If you're building a RAG system, don't search for an existing RAG benchmark—build your own evaluation instead.

sources.quote: [illustrative] a generic RAG leaderboard won't tell you if YOUR retrieval works
sources.statement: [illustrative] Custom evals beat generic benchmarks for retrieval systems.

status_history.reason: stated in the ingested evals talk
a second source agreed within three months

positions.statement: Manual evaluation is the right place to start; automation scales human judgment but does not replace it.

sources.quote: The first obvious solution to this complexity is manual evaluations, and honestly that's where you should start.
sources.statement: Manual evaluation—reading outputs yourself—is the right place to start, since it builds intuition, reveals patterns, and clarifies what 'good' means for your use case.

sources.quote: Automated evaluations are there to scale your judgment, not to replace it. If you don't know yet what you're evaluating manually, there is nothing to automate.
sources.statement: Automated evaluations exist to scale human judgment, not replace it—if you haven't figured out what to evaluate manually first, there's nothing meaningful to automate.

status_history.reason: single source so far — genuinely open

positions.statement: LLM-as-a-judge is reliable enough to depend on for evaluating LLM outputs.

sources.quote: And it works surprisingly well. Just remember that your LLM judge is like a small machine learning project in itself and it also requires some tuning and evaluation.
sources.statement: LLM-as-a-judge works surprisingly well, but the judge itself is like a small ML project that requires its own tuning and evaluation.

sources.quote: [illustrative] an uncalibrated LLM judge is confidently wrong; don't trust it raw
sources.statement: [illustrative] LLM-as-a-judge is NOT reliable without heavy calibration.
